The rule states that the groundspeed of the small unmanned aircraft may not exceed 87 knots (100 miles per hour), and that the altitude may not be higher than 400 feet above ground level unless the aircraft is flown within a 400-foot radius of a structure and does not fly higher than 400 feet above that structure's immediate uppermost limit.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-107.51
questionText: Under 14 CFR part 107, what is the maximum groundspeed permitted for a small unmanned aircraft?
answers: 87 knots (100 miles per hour)
100 knots (115 miles per hour)
45 knots (52 miles per hour)
There is no groundspeed limit below 400 feet AGL
correctAnswer: 87 knots (100 miles per hour)
hint: The limit in 107.51 is stated in knots first, with the equivalent in miles per hour in parentheses.
explanation: 107.51 caps groundspeed at 87 knots, which the rule then restates as 100 miles per hour. The two figures describe the same limit in different units, so an answer pairing 100 with knots inflates it by roughly 15 percent. The cap applies regardless of altitude — there is no band low enough to fly out from under it.

questionText: A remote pilot wants to inspect the top of a 900-foot tower. What does part 107 allow?
answers: Flight up to 1,300 feet AGL, provided the aircraft stays within a 400-foot radius of the tower
Flight up to 400 feet AGL only, because the 400-foot ceiling has no exceptions
Flight up to 900 feet AGL anywhere within one statute mile of the tower
Flight to any altitude, because structure inspection is exempt from altitude limits
correctAnswer: Flight up to 1,300 feet AGL, provided the aircraft stays within a 400-foot radius of the tower
hint: The structure exception allows 400 feet above the structure's uppermost limit, and confines the aircraft to a 400-foot radius of it.
explanation: The structure exception in 107.51 does not lift the ceiling, it moves it: you may fly up to 400 feet above the structure's uppermost limit, which for a 900-foot tower is 1,300 feet AGL. The permission is bought with proximity — stray beyond a 400-foot radius of the tower and the ordinary 400-foot AGL ceiling applies again.

questionText: What are the minimum cloud clearance requirements for a small unmanned aircraft operated under part 107?

1,000 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontally
500 feet below and 1,000 feet horizontally
Clear of clouds in all directions

questionText: A small unmanned aircraft is destroyed on impact and also breaks a $200 window. No one is injured. What reporting is required?

questionText: Who is directly responsible for and the final authority as to the operation of a small unmanned aircraft system?

The person manipulating the flight controls
The owner of the aircraft

questionText: After deviating from a rule of part 107 to meet an in-flight emergency, what must the remote pilot in command do?

Most small unmanned aircraft systems are programmed with a predetermined behaviour when the control link is lost — returning to the launch point, hovering, or landing — so the remote pilot is expected to know what the aircraft will do before the flight begins.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-107.19
questionText: Why should a remote pilot know the aircraft's programmed lost link behaviour before flight?
answers: So the area the aircraft will fly to or land in can be assessed and kept clear beforehand
So the lost link event does not have to be reported to the FAA
So the control link can be re-established from a second control station
So the aircraft can be flown beyond visual line of sight once the behaviour is known

hint: The value of knowing the behaviour is that it makes the outcome of a lost link predictable on the ground.
explanation: Because the behaviour is decided by the manufacturer in advance and executes without you. Knowing whether the aircraft will hover, return to its launch point, or land where it stands is what lets you keep that path and that ground clear — which is how 107.19(c)'s duty to pose no undue hazard on loss of control is actually discharged.

Without limit, until the aircraft is on the ground
Only within the limits of a pre-issued certificate of waiver
Only with prior approval from Air Traffic Control

questionText: A small unmanned aircraft stops responding to control inputs and flies away from the operating site. What should the remote pilot in command do first?

Immediately power off the control station to conserve its battery
Wait until the aircraft's battery is exhausted before taking any action
Launch a second aircraft to follow and observe the first

Protecting people and other aircraft in its path — warning those at risk, and alerting ATC if it is heading for controlled airspace — is what 107.19(c) makes the pilot responsible for. questionText: What characterizes a suitable emergency landing site chosen during preflight planning?
answers: It is clear of people and property and reachable from the planned flight area
It is the nearest paved surface, regardless of who is on it
It is directly beneath the highest point of the planned route
It is within the boundary of the nearest airport

Many small unmanned aircraft rely on satellite positioning for station keeping and return-to-home, so when GPS reception degrades the aircraft may drift with the wind and position-dependent features become unreliable.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
questionText: A small unmanned aircraft loses GPS reception in flight. What is the most likely immediate effect?
answers: The aircraft may drift with the wind and position-holding features may become unreliable
The control link is lost and the aircraft will land immediately
The aircraft's maximum altitude is automatically reduced to 400 feet AGL
The motors shut down to prevent an uncontrolled flyaway
correctAnswer: The aircraft may drift with the wind and position-holding features may become unreliable
hint: Satellite positioning is what holds the aircraft in place; the control link is a separate system.
explanation: GPS feeds position holding, not propulsion or the control link. Losing it typically drops the aircraft into an attitude-only mode where it drifts with the wind and holds station poorly, while still answering the sticks. The motors do not stop and the link is unaffected, which is why the failure can go unnoticed until the aircraft is somewhere unintended.

Only when a visual observer is being used

A report to Air Traffic Control before the next flight

Source: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
questionText: A remote pilot notices that a lithium battery pack has swollen since its last use. What is the appropriate action?
answers: Remove the battery from service and do not fly it
Fly it once more at reduced power to discharge it safely in flight
Charge it fully, since swelling indicates a low state of charge
Continue using it until the flight time noticeably decreases
correctAnswer: Remove the battery from service and do not fly it
hint: Swelling is one of the recognized signs of a failing cell, and a failing cell is not made safer by another flight.
explanation: Swelling is gas from internal breakdown, and it is one of the recognized precursors to a lithium fire — along with punctures, physical damage, overcharging and overheating. It is a one-way change, so there is no safe last flight and no charge cycle that reverses it. The pack comes out of service.
